title: Molihua (Jasmine Flower)
origin: Jiangsu folk song of the Qing dynasty, the best known Chinese melody outside China

pd.detail: Anonymous Jiangsu folk melody in circulation by the Qianlong era (1736-1795); earliest Western printing is the air 'Moo-Lee-Chwa' in John Barrow, Travels in China, London 1804.
pd.sourceEdition: Standard Jiangsu variant in the anhemitonic pentatonic on C (1 2 3 5 6), from public-domain reference notation (jianpu) of the traditional melody
pd.notes: The traditional jianpu is barred in 2/4; encoded here as 4/4 with two written bars per encoded bar, so the quarter-note pulse is unchanged and no note is rebarred off its beat. The words carry their own separate PD basis on each section (see section.lyrics.pd) and come from Barrow's 1804 printing, not from the modern wording. The original is an unaccompanied pentatonic tune - the chords here are a light supporting harmonisation, not part of the composition. The head cadences on degree 3 and the tune as a whole closes on the low degree 5, which is the zhi-mode ending of the Jiangsu version.

pd.detail: Anonymous Jiangsu folk text with no named author at any stage of its transmission; Barrow heard it in 1793-94 and reports it as one of the most popular songs in the whole country.
pd.sourceEdition: John Barrow, Travels in China, London 1804, pp. 316-317 - the air 'Moo-lee-wha', stanza I on p. 316 and stanza II on p. 317, in Barrow's own romanization

lyrics.notes: Transcribed verbatim from Barrow's 1804 romanization, which is why the spelling is his and not pinyin (checked line by line against the 1804 first edition and the 1806 reprint). The wording sung today is a 1950s edit and is deliberately NOT used. Barrow prints exactly two stanzas of four lines each, with no repeat marks; both stanzas are encoded in full, so nothing is omitted, and there is nothing offensive in either. Line 1 is set twice here because this phrase is written out twice note-for-note in the melody above. Barrow's facing literal English translation is not encoded - the schema wants transliteration, not a singing translation.

pd.detail: Anonymous Jiangsu folk text with no named author at any stage of its transmission; Barrow heard it in 1793-94 and reports it as one of the most popular songs in the whole country.
pd.sourceEdition: John Barrow, Travels in China, London 1804, pp. 316-317 - the air 'Moo-lee-wha', stanza I on p. 316 and stanza II on p. 317, in Barrow's own romanization

lyrics.notes: Lines 2 and 3 of each Barrow stanza. Line 2 sits on the eight-note phrase in bars 0-1, which carries its eight syllables one to one; line 3 enters at bar 2, after the held degree 5 that closes the first phrase.

stanzas.text: Yeu tchau yeu jie lo tsai go kia
Go pun tai, poo tchoo mun
Man yuen wha kai soy poo quee ta
Go pun tai tsai ye ta

lyrics.notes: The closing line 4 of each Barrow stanza only. From bar 2 the bridge is deliberately left wordless: that is the descending zhi-mode tail, and since Barrow prints neither a fifth line nor a repeat mark, nothing is invented to fill it.

stanzas.text: Twee tcho sien wha ul lo.
Tai you kung kan wha jin ma.
